pumac-2011-combinatorics-a-05.title: Tail sums of the expectation
pumac-2011-combinatorics-a-05.body:
Let $n=7$ and $E[L]=\sum_{l\ge1}\Pr[L\ge l]$.

$L\ge1$ means the first entry is not $0$: probability $\tfrac{n-1}{n}$.
For $l\ge2$, $L\ge l$ means the first $l$ entries are $l$ consecutive integers (none equal to $0$), in increasing or decreasing order. There are $n-l$ possible starting values ($1,\dots,n-l$ for the increasing case, mirrored for the decreasing case), and the remaining $n-l$ entries can be arranged in $(n-l)!$ ways, so
$$\Pr[L\ge l]=\frac{2(n-l)\,(n-l)!}{n!}.$$
Then with $n=7$,
$$E[L]=\frac67+\frac{2}{7!}\sum_{l=2}^{7}(7-l)(7-l)!=\frac67+\frac2{5040}\sum_{j=1}^{5}j\cdot j!.$$
Since $\sum_{j=1}^{5}j\cdot j!=\sum_{j=1}^5\big((j+1)!-j!\big)=6!-1=719$,
$$E[L]=\frac{4320+1438}{5040}=\frac{5758}{5040}=\frac{2879}{2520}.$$
This is in lowest terms ($2879$ is prime to $2520=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7$), so $m+n=2879+2520=5399$.

**Answer: 5399**

pumac-2011-combinatorics-a-05.title: Exhaustive check
pumac-2011-combinatorics-a-05.body:
Listing all $5040$ permutations of $\{0,\dots,6\}$ and adding up $L(\sigma)$ (using the rule that $L$ counts the maximal run of consecutive integers, increasing or decreasing, at the start, stopping before a $0$) gives total $\tfrac{2879}{2520}\cdot5040=5758$, so $E[L]=\tfrac{2879}{2520}$ and the answer is $5399$.

**Answer: 5399**

pumac-2011-combinatorics-a-08.title: Trees and double stars
pumac-2011-combinatorics-a-08.body:
Condition (1) says the highway network is connected with a unique path between any two cities, i.e. it is a **tree** on $21$ vertices ($20$ highways). A trip through exactly $5$ cities is a path with $4$ edges, counted once for each direction, so $N=2P_4(T)$ where $P_4(T)$ is the number of undirected $4$-edge paths.

**Structure of an optimal tree.** Take a tree maximizing $P_4$. If $v,w$ are leaves whose distance is not $4$, no $4$-path contains both of them. Let $n_4(x)$ be the number of vertices at distance $4$ from $x$. Deleting $v$ and attaching a new leaf to the neighbour of $w$ changes $P_4$ by $n_4(w)-n_4(v)$, so by maximality $n_4(v)=n_4(w)$ for all such pairs. Repeating this "move a leaf next to another leaf" operation merges leaves that are at distance neither $2$ nor $4$ into the same family without lowering $P_4$, so we may assume any two leaves are at distance $2$ or $4$. Such a tree is a centre $v$ with $m$ neighbours $v_1,\dots,v_m$, where $v_i$ carries $p_i$ pendant leaves.

**Counting.** The $4$-paths are exactly leaf $-v_i-v-v_j-$ leaf with $i<j$, so
$$P_4=\sum_{i<j}p_ip_j,\qquad 1+m+\sum p_i=21.$$
For fixed $m$ and fixed $\sum p_i=20-m$, the sum is maximized when the $p_i$ are as equal as possible. Checking:

| $m$ | $p_i$ | $P_4$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 9, 9 | 81 |
| 3 | 6, 6, 5 | 96 |
| 4 | 4, 4, 4, 4 | 96 |
| 5 | 3, 3, 3, 3, 3 | 90 |
| 6 | 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2 | 81 |

and $P_4$ decreases further for larger $m$. So the maximum is $P_4=96$ and $N=2\cdot96=192$.

**Answer: 192**
